rationale: The book's core identification—that righteousness is the doing of God's commandments (the law kept as righteous acts)—is carried more directly and consistently by the definitional texts it cites and by the garment symbol than the dominant status/imputation reading. Deut 6:25, Ps 119:172 and 1 John 3:7 function as explicit equations of righteousness with observance and doing; Rev 19:8 (dikaiōmata) further identifies the wedding garment itself as the saints' righteous acts. These cannot be reduced to mere evidence or fruit without forcing the grammar. The common forensic reading better accounts for certain Pauline contrasts, yet those can be read consistently with the prior-accepted premises (belief and faith already include obedient submission) and with the book's own insistence that the acts are God-given and blood-washed rather than self-generated. Secondary elaborations (precise garment mechanics, covenant-skirt imagery, daily foot-washing) are plausible extensions but not indispensable to the core. No counter-reading explains the same definitional cluster plus the garment texts with fewer unsupported steps.
book_core_identification: Righteousness is the doing of God's commandments—the law kept, the performance of righteous acts.
book_secondary_elaborations: Worn as the garment of righteous acts (Rev 19:8 dikaiōmata; wedding garment of Matt 22)
Not a vague goodness nor a verdict only received
Granted/ordained by God (Eph 2:10) yet put on and kept by the wearer
Covenant covering that both clothes and must be washed clean of defilement
Opposite of nakedness/shame and of self-made fig-leaf coverings
strongest_counter_interpretation: Righteousness primarily denotes a forensic/legal status of right standing before God that is imputed or credited to the believer through faith in Christ apart from works of the law; ethical doing is the subsequent fruit or evidence of that status rather than its definition.
counter_core_identification: Right standing before God (justification status) credited through faith, not the performance of commandments itself.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that righteousness is essentially identical with the doing of the commandments; it treats the doing texts as secondary or evidential while elevating the imputed status as the primary soteriological referent.
counter_case: Gen 15:6 / Rom 4:3–8: Abraham’s faith is counted as righteousness apart from works
Rom 3:21–26; Phil 3:9: righteousness of God manifested and received through faith in Christ, not one’s own from the law
2 Cor 5:21: believers become the righteousness of God in him
Isa 64:6 and the broader Protestant tradition read ‘righteousnesses as filthy rags’ as undercutting any claim that law-keeping constitutes righteousness
Common reading of the wedding garment as Christ’s imputed righteousness supplied by the king rather than the guest’s own acts
book_explanatory_advantages: Direct equative statements (Deut 6:25 ‘it shall be our righteousness if we observe to do’; Ps 119:172 ‘all thy commandments are righteousness’; 1 John 3:7 ‘he that doeth righteousness is righteous’) require no redefinition of ‘is’
Rev 19:8 explicitly equates the fine linen with the righteous acts (plural, active) of the saints, matching the garment symbolism
Consistent with prior-accepted cores (love = keeping commandments; faith and belief include obedient submission; knowing proven by obedience)
Handles ‘filthy rags’ contextually as stained-by-sin rather than inherently filthy obedience, and supplies the washing remedy already present in Isaiah and Revelation
Unifies OT law language with NT garment and armor imagery without reversing the direction of scriptural witness
counter_explanatory_advantages: Accounts more immediately for the dense Pauline cluster that contrasts ‘righteousness of faith’ with ‘righteousness of the law/works’
Matches the historic Protestant forensic emphasis and the ‘credited/counted’ vocabulary of Genesis–Romans
Explains why many readers instinctively treat the wedding garment as an alien covering supplied by the host
unresolved_objections: Full integration of the ‘apart from works’ and ‘not my own righteousness’ language in Romans 4 and Philippians 3 still requires the prior premises on faith/belief to avoid tension
Secondary garment and washing elaborations, while coherent, rest on additional symbolic chains that are not strictly required by the three printed definitional texts
